issues.legal_issue: A landlord seeking possession for a proposed self-employment business need not prove in advance that the landlord has the funds or prior experience required to start that business.
material_facts: The landlord sought possession so his technically qualified son could start a computer consultancy business.
The landlord produced records of ownership of agricultural land and stated that he could raise funds from financial institutions.
The courts below rejected the claim in part because they considered the landlord unable to generate the funds required to start the business.
issues.conclusion: The courts below relied on an irrelevant consideration in requiring proof of financial capacity; the finding on that point was unsustainable.
issues.legal_principle: Section 21(1)(a) of the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Lettings, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 permits eviction for a bona fide need for a profession, trade or calling. Under Dattatraya Laxman Kamble v. Abdul Rasul Moulali Kotkunde, a landlord must prove the asserted need, but there is no presumption that it is not bona fide; doubts may be put to the landlord to clear. Raghunath G. Panhale v. Chaganlal Sundarji and Co. holds that a landlord need not prove money to invest in a contemplated business or experience in that business.

predicates.eviction_application_for_nonresidential_: A landlord applied to evict a tenant from premises let for use in a nonresidential business or occupation.
predicates.proposed_self_employment_business: The landlord proposed that a family member use the premises to start a business for self-employment.
predicates.court_rejects_need_for_lack_of_startup_f: The court treated the landlord's lack of proven startup funds or business experience as a reason to reject the claimed need.

issues.definition: When a landlord's nonresidential eviction claim rests on a proposed self-employment business and the court rejects it for want of proven funds or experience, those matters need not be proved.

issues.legal_issue: Withdrawal of a proposed franchise does not by itself defeat a bona fide need to start an independently planned business in the premises.
material_facts: After filing the eviction application, the landlord applied for a franchise for the proposed computer consultancy centre.
The franchise was granted and later withdrawn.
The landlord stated that his son intended to start the business independently and that the franchise application was made to improve its viability, not because the business depended on a franchise.
The son held a postgraduate diploma in computer science.
issues.conclusion: The withdrawal of the franchise did not justify concluding that the son could not start the proposed business or that the premises were not bona fide required.
issues.legal_principle: Section 21(1)(a) of the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Lettings, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 requires a bona fide need; such need must be honest and not a mere desire or wish. Whether the business depends on a franchise must be assessed against the landlord's stated plan and the evidence, rather than inferred from the withdrawal of a franchise when the business was not said to depend on it.

rule.if: eviction_application_for_nonresidential_use and independent_business_plan and franchise_withdrawn and business_not_conditional_on_franchise

predicates.eviction_application_for_nonresidential_: A landlord applied to evict a tenant so the premises could be used for a nonresidential business or occupation.
predicates.independent_business_plan: The landlord stated that the proposed business would be started independently of any franchise.
predicates.franchise_withdrawn: A franchise sought for the proposed business was later withdrawn.
predicates.business_not_conditional_on_franchise: The landlord did not claim that the business could be started only if a franchise were obtained.

issues.definition: If a landlord seeks premises for an independently planned business and a proposed franchise is withdrawn but was not a condition of starting the business, the withdrawal does not defeat the bona fide need.

issues.legal_issue: A separate affidavit from a family member proposing to run a business is not necessary where the family member's qualification is evidenced and the landlord makes a categorical statement that the family member will run it.
material_facts: The landlord's son held a postgraduate diploma in computer science, and a copy of the diploma was filed.
The landlord categorically stated that his son would run the proposed business in the premises.
The courts below treated the absence of an affidavit from the son about his technical knowledge and inclination as adverse to the claim.
issues.conclusion: The courts below erred in treating the absence of the son's affidavit as a reason to reject the need.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 21(1)(a) of the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Lettings, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, bona fide need is assessed on the evidence of the claimed requirement. Where documentary evidence establishes the family member's technical qualification and the landlord categorically states that the family member will run the business, a separate affidavit from that family member is not necessary to establish technical knowledge and inclination.

predicates.eviction_application_for_family_member_b: A landlord applied to evict a tenant so a family member could use the premises for a business.
predicates.qualification_documented: Documentary evidence was provided of the family member's relevant technical qualification.
predicates.landlord_categorically_identifies_family: The landlord stated categorically that the family member would operate the proposed business.
predicates.separate_affidavit_absent: The family member did not file a separate affidavit about technical knowledge or willingness to run the business.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks premises for a family member's business, documents establish the member's qualification and the landlord identifies that member as the operator, the absence of a separate affidavit does not prevent the need from being established.

issues.legal_issue: Failure to start a proposed business from other rented premises while eviction proceedings are pending does not defeat the claimed need when the application identified the premises in dispute as the intended location.
material_facts: The landlord stated that the business was to be started in the premises in dispute and that he could not take other premises on rent.
The son did not start the business from rented premises during the years after the eviction application was filed.
The courts below treated that failure as evidence that the premises were not needed.
issues.conclusion: The failure to start the business from another rented premises was not a valid ground to deny eviction.
issues.legal_principle: The crucial date for deciding the bona fides of a landlord's requirement is the date the eviction application is filed. Gaya Prasad v. Pradeep Srivastava applied that principle and declined to treat later events during lengthy litigation as negating the need existing on the filing date.

predicates.eviction_application_for_proposed_busine: A landlord applied to evict a tenant to use the premises for a proposed business.
predicates.application_identifies_disputed_premises: The landlord stated that the proposed business was to be started in the premises in dispute.
predicates.business_not_started_in_other_rented_pre: The proposed business was not started from other rented premises while the eviction case was pending.

issues.definition: If the eviction application identifies the disputed premises as the intended business location, not starting the business from another rented premises during the litigation does not defeat the need.

issues.legal_issue: A technically educated family member's need for self-employment must receive due consideration where the family member completed the education after the building was first let, is not employed in government service, and wants to engage in self-employment.
material_facts: The landlord's son was a minor when the premises were let.
After the building was let, the son completed a postgraduate diploma in computer science.
The son was not employed in government service and was proposed to engage in self-employment by starting a computer consultancy business.
The courts below did not apply the criteria in Rule 16(2)(d).
issues.conclusion: All the criteria in Rule 16(2)(d) were proved, and the son's need was entitled to due consideration; the landlord was entitled to an eviction decree.
issues.legal_principle: Section 21(1)(a) of the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Lettings, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 provides for eviction on a landlord's bona fide need, including for a family member's profession, trade or calling. Rule 16(2)(d) of the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent or Eviction) Rules, 1972 requires due consideration for the need of a son who completed technical education after the building was let, is not employed in government service, and wants to engage in self-employment.

predicates.eviction_application_for_family_member_s: A landlord applied to evict a tenant so a family member could use the premises for self-employment.
predicates.family_member_completed_technical_educat: The family member completed technical education after the building was first let.
predicates.family_member_not_in_government_service: The family member was not employed in government service.
predicates.family_member_wants_self_employment: The family member wanted to engage in self-employment.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks premises for a family member who meets the stated education, employment and self-employment facts, that need receives due consideration.

issues.legal_issue: Comparative hardship favors eviction where refusal would leave the landlord without premises for the proposed business while the tenant has other business premises and uses the disputed premises only for storage.
material_facts: The landlord had no other premises for his son's proposed business.
The tenant had purchased adjoining property, had other premises from which he ran his business, and used the disputed premises only to store spare parts.
The tenant was described as a prosperous businessman.
issues.conclusion: The landlord would suffer greater hardship if eviction were refused.
issues.legal_principle: In assessing the parties' circumstances on the eviction claim, the Court compared the hardship that refusal or grant of eviction would cause. It found greater hardship to the landlord because he had no alternative premises for the proposed business, whereas the tenant had other premises for his business and used the disputed premises only for storage.

rule.if: eviction_application_for_proposed_business and landlord_has_no_alternative_premises and tenant_has_other_business_premises and disputed_premises_used_only_for_storage

predicates.eviction_application_for_proposed_busine: A landlord applied to evict a tenant so the premises could be used for a proposed business.
predicates.landlord_has_no_alternative_premises: The landlord had no other premises available for the proposed business.
predicates.tenant_has_other_business_premises: The tenant had other premises from which the tenant ran the business.
predicates.disputed_premises_used_only_for_storage: The tenant used the premises in dispute only to store goods or parts.

issues.definition: When the landlord lacks alternative premises, the tenant has other business premises, and the disputed premises are used only for storage, the hardship balance favors eviction.
